strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: reducing the annotation bottleneck for multi-hop QA by generating bridge and comparison questions directly from unstructured corpora without per-example knowledge graphs or hand-built question templates.

HopWeaver is a coherent end-to-end system combining complementary-document retrieval, diversity-aware MMR, a reranker fine-tuned with simulated feedback, sub-question composition, and a separate polishing/validation stage.

The framework explicitly represents reasoning paths and formulates cross-document constraints for both bridge and comparison questions, which makes the intended multi-hop structure more interpretable than in many synthetic-data pipelines.

The evaluation is unusually broad: it combines LLM-as-judge scoring, Q-only versus Q+Docs answerability, evidence-retrieval metrics, reranker and polisher ablations, multiple generator scales, and cost analysis.

The reported Q-only to Q+Docs improvements provide evidence that the generated questions benefit from supporting documents, while the reranker ablation shows improved retrieval success and fewer attempts. The cost analysis also supports practical scalability.

The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful pipeline diagrams, generated examples, detailed experimental settings, and extensive prompt appendices. The inclusion of open-source generators improves accessibility and reproducibility relative to proprietary-only evaluations.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated. The descriptions 'first automatic framework,' 'without human intervention,' and effectiveness 'in specialized domains' are not fully substantiated: the system requires substantial prompt, threshold, and pipeline engineering, and all quantitative experiments use English Wikipedia rather than specialized-domain corpora.

The claim that synthesized questions meet or exceed human-annotated datasets rests almost entirely on LLM-as-judge scores. Judge self-consistency and inter-run reliability do not establish external validity, and no independent human evaluation of factuality, naturalness, or genuine multi-hop necessity is provided. The reliability analysis also does not eliminate possible length, style, or model-family biases.

The main comparisons use only 100 samples and report no confidence intervals or significance tests. The human-annotated baselines differ in domain, difficulty, reasoning length, and annotation protocol, and MusiQue lacks comparison-question results, so the aggregate superiority claim is not conclusive.

The multi-hop constraints are conceptual rather than formally enforced by the implementation. They are largely checked by LLMs, and questions about famous entities may still be answerable directly from model world knowledge. The Q-only/Q+Docs gap shows that documents are useful, but it does not prove that every question requires the intended cross-document reasoning chain.

Answerability with golden documents is partly circular because those documents are the same sources used to generate the questions. Meanwhile, evidence retrieval is imperfect—for example, BM25 Recall@20 is about 0.705 and Support F1 is only 0.2217—but no end-to-end retrieved-document reader is evaluated, leaving practical RAG performance unclear.

The paper omits important dataset-level statistics such as total generated questions, acceptance/rejection yields, entity and relation distributions, document-distance distributions, and large-scale failure or hallucination rates. This makes it difficult to judge robustness beyond the evaluated samples.

The method is highly dependent on a sequence of LLM calls and prompts. Although open models are included, the strongest results rely on proprietary APIs whose behavior can change; more detail on data release, reranker training data, and reproducible snapshots would strengthen the artifact.

Some formalization is imprecise, such as the apparent typo in Equation (6) and the lack of a precise algorithmic description of how the Fact Distribution, No-Shortcut, and Distributed Source constraints are verified. The technical novelty is also primarily an integration of existing retrieval, reranking, and LLM self-refinement components rather than a fundamentally new reasoning mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses an important MHQA bottleneck: reducing the cost and manual effort required to create cross-document bridge and comparison questions.

The proposed pipeline is coherent and reasonably complete, covering bridge-entity identification, diversity-aware retrieval, reranking, sub-question generation, question fusion, comparison-entity discovery, polishing, and validation.

The evaluation is broader than a single quality score: it combines LLM-as-judge ratings, Q-only versus Q+Docs solver performance, evidence-retrieval metrics, reranker and polisher ablations, multiple generators and solvers, and a cost analysis.

Reproducibility is aided by the named Wikipedia snapshot, preprocessing rules, model versions, embedding and reranker models, retrieval parameters, deterministic generation settings, appendix prompts, use of open-source models, and promised code release.

The figures and appendix examples make the intended reasoning paths interpretable, and the reported Q+Docs improvements are consistent with the claim that supporting evidence helps answer the generated questions.
weaknesses: The central claim that synthesized questions match or exceed human-annotated datasets is supported almost entirely by LLM judges. Self-consistency across repeated runs measures reliability, not validity; without an independent human or expert audit, systematic judge bias, preference for LLM style, or benchmark contamination cannot be ruled out.

The experiments do not directly prove that both documents are necessary. Q-only versus Q+Docs shows that evidence helps, but source-only, target-only, both-documents, counterfactual-document, and repeated-evidence conditions are needed. The formal constraints over extracted triplets do not prevent single-document inference, parametric knowledge, or redundant information from yielding the answer.

The main evaluations use only 100 samples, with no confidence intervals or significance tests. Several claimed advantages over human datasets are small, such as average scores around 4.27 versus 4.23, and dataset-level statistics such as total generation count, acceptance yield, duplication, and coverage are absent.

Generalization is overstated. All systematic experiments use the English Wikipedia general-domain corpus, despite claims about specialized domains; the title refers to multiple corpora although only one corpus is used; and the system handles only two-hop questions while being compared with datasets such as MuSiQue that contain longer reasoning chains.

The formalization has several gaps and inconsistencies. It is unclear how E, R, and Trips(d) are populated or how the constraints are algorithmically enforced; Eq. (3) appears to require global uniqueness of a triplet rather than merely assigning it to one supporting document; path indexing is inconsistent; and the reranker is trained with the bridge entity while retrieval is described as using the generated query q.

The evidence-accessibility results are open to alternative interpretations. Very low Support F1 scores of roughly 0.17–0.22 may reflect genuine multi-source difficulty, but they could also indicate retrieval failures, granularity mismatches, or poorly localized evidence. No end-to-end retrieve-then-answer evaluation is reported.

The reranker and polisher ablations rely on indirect or circular signals. Reranker labels are derived from whether an LLM can subsequently form a question, so valid complementary documents may be treated as negatives; the reported reranker gain is only 1.3 percentage points; and polisher improvements are assessed by the same type of LLM-based evaluation used throughout the paper.

The wording “first framework” and “without human intervention or structured data” is too absolute. The system relies on substantial human prompt engineering and on LLMs pretrained on human-authored and possibly structured/benchmark data. These claims should be narrowed or more carefully differentiated from prior work.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in multi-hop question answering: expensive annotation and the difficulty of obtaining questions that genuinely require cross-document reasoning.

HopWeaver is a coherent end-to-end pipeline combining complementary-document retrieval, MMR-style diversity, a simulated-feedback reranker, sub-question decomposition and fusion, explicit reasoning paths, and polishing/validation.

The framework targets two practically important MHQA patterns—bridge and comparison questions—and produces interpretable verification artifacts such as source spans, sub-questions, answers, and reasoning paths.

The evaluation is unusually broad for a synthesis paper: it uses multiple generators, an LLM-judge ensemble, Q-only versus Q+Docs conditions, retrieval/accessibility metrics, reranker and polisher ablations, and a detailed cost analysis.
Reproducibility is supported by public code, extensive prompt appendices, hyperparameter settings, model specifications, and comparisons with both closed-source and open-source generators.

The reported empirical patterns are consistent with the intended design: providing golden evidence substantially improves answers, weaker models benefit greatly from the evidence, and both the reranker and polisher improve synthesis efficiency or quality.
weaknesses: The central claim that synthesized questions meet or exceed human-annotated datasets relies almost entirely on LLM-as-judge scores. Self-consistency establishes reliability, not validity, and without an independent human audit or factuality check, the judges may favor fluent LLM-generated questions or share model-family biases.

The main quality and answerability evaluations use only 100 samples and report no confidence intervals or significance tests. Several advantages over human datasets are small, such as 4.27 versus 4.23 average quality for bridge questions, so the superiority claim is not strongly established.

The practical dataset-construction value is not demonstrated end to end. The Q+Docs setting supplies golden documents, while no realistic retrieval-augmented setting or downstream training experiment shows that synthetic questions improve MHQA systems.

The raw-corpus-only claim is somewhat overstated. In particular, comparison-question Direct Recommendation can select a comparable entity from the LLM's parametric knowledge before retrieval, and the system depends on LLM-generated structured triplets even if no external knowledge graph is used.

The formal constraints do not fully guarantee the intended cross-document property. For a two-triplet bridge path, Equation (3) does not explicitly require the triplets to occur in different documents, while Equation (4) is vacuous for two-hop paths because there are no non-adjacent entity pairs.

Entity normalization, cross-document coreference, and global triplet construction are under-specified. The constraints are only as reliable as the LLM extractor and may not be deterministically enforced over the full corpus.

The evidence-accessibility results are open to alternative interpretations. Low Support F1 and imperfect Recall@20 may indicate genuine multi-source difficulty, but they could also reflect ambiguous or poorly selected evidence; the paper does not provide a quantified manual analysis separating these explanations.

Generalization is limited to English Wikipedia and two-hop bridge/comparison patterns. The claimed value for specialized domains and scarce-annotation settings is not empirically tested, and longer reasoning chains or other MHQA patterns are excluded.

There are minor reproducibility inconsistencies in model naming, including Qwen3-8B versus Qwen3-9B and Qwen-14B versus Qwen3-14B. The exact released dataset size and sampling protocol for baseline comparisons should also be made more prominent.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: scalable, corpus-only generation of bridge and comparison multi-hop questions for evaluating LLMs and RAG systems.

The HopWeaver pipeline is detailed and coherent, covering bridge-entity identification, diversity-aware retrieval, reranking, sub-question composition, comparison-attribute filtering, and final polishing and validation.

The evaluation is broader than a single LLM-as-judge score: it includes answerability under Q-Only and Q+Docs conditions, evidence-accessibility metrics, manual reasoning-path checks, and end-to-end evaluation of multiple RAG methods.

Reproducibility is supported by corpus dates, model specifications, retrieval parameters, deterministic generation settings, extensive prompt examples, cost analysis, and a stated public code release.

The reported gains from adding gold documents and the low end-to-end RAG scores provide evidence that the synthesized questions can require genuine evidence integration and can serve as challenging evaluation data.
weaknesses: Claims that HopWeaver meets or exceeds human-annotated benchmarks rely mainly on 100-sample evaluations with no confidence intervals or significance tests; several score differences are very small, and the truncated radar chart can exaggerate them. The 500-sample follow-up uses only one generator and does not fully resolve this concern.

LLM-as-judge validity remains a central risk. Judge selection emphasizes self-consistency, while human validation is limited to pairwise preferences and shows only moderate inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' Kappa 0.46). Closed-source judges also limit exact reproducibility, and the reported 92%/94% human-alignment figures are inconsistent.

The formal fact-distribution, no-shortcut, and distributed-source constraints are largely enforced through LLM prompts rather than deterministic or adversarial checks. There is no direct per-document unanswerability test or systematic shortcut evaluation to prove that every question truly requires both documents.

The simulated supervision for reranker fine-tuning can be noisy: a failed generation attempt may reflect LLM errors rather than a non-complementary document. Training with the bridge entity as the query also differs from the expanded retrieval query used in the pipeline, and the consequences of this mismatch are not analyzed.

The paper does not directly compare against prior synthetic-question frameworks, which makes the 'first' and superiority claims harder to assess. It also does not measure topic, entity, template, or lexical diversity, leaving possible repetition unexamined.

External validity is limited: experiments use only English Wikipedia, remove long articles, and do not demonstrate the claimed benefit in specialized or low-resource domains. Lower cost relative to human annotation is inferred from API pricing rather than measured against an annotation workflow.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: reducing the cost of constructing multi-hop QA datasets while aiming to avoid pseudo-multi-hop questions.

The proposed framework is clearly organized into bridge and comparison pipelines, with retrieval, reranking, question construction, polishing, and validation. The formal definitions and Figure 2 make the overall process understandable.

The evaluation is broader than typical question-generation studies, combining LLM-as-judge scores, Q-only versus Q+Docs answerability, retrieval metrics, and end-to-end RAG evaluation across several open and proprietary models.
The authors include reranker and polisher ablations, a 500-sample stability study, manual inspection of reasoning paths, error analysis, cost analysis, and substantial prompt documentation.
The use of reasoning paths and source-specific sub-questions is a sensible design choice for improving interpretability and verifying where the required evidence comes from.
weaknesses: The central claim of authentic multi-hop reasoning is not established rigorously enough. The Fact Distribution and No-Shortcut constraints are formalized, but the manuscript does not show an executable, corpus-level verifier; enforcement is largely left to LLMs. There is also no single-document oracle condition showing that neither supporting document alone is sufficient.

Q-only versus Q+Docs only demonstrates that providing evidence improves performance. It does not prove that both documents are necessary, so questions may still contain shortcuts or be answerable from one document plus parametric knowledge.

The quality evaluation is potentially circular because questions are generated by LLMs and then evaluated primarily by other LLMs. Self-consistency measures repeatability, not validity, and LLM judges may systematically prefer fluent or verbose synthetic questions.

The human validation is too limited to validate the strong superiority claims: it uses 50 selected pairwise comparisons, three computer-science students, and reports only moderate inter-rater agreement, with Fleiss' Kappa of 0.46. It does not validate the absolute pointwise scores or all evaluation dimensions.

The main comparison uses only 100 samples per source and reports no confidence intervals or significance tests. Several score differences over human datasets are small, around 0.2 on a 1-5 scale, yet are described as surpassing human benchmarks.

The paper does not experimentally compare HopWeaver against prior automated synthesis frameworks, such as Source2Synth, MINTQA, KGAST, or the MuSiQue construction pipeline, under the same corpus and settings. Comparison with human datasets alone cannot substantiate the claim that this is the best or first fully automatic approach.

Manual inspection found that only 92% of reasoning paths were correct, with information-gap, ambiguity, and factual-reasoning errors. The very low Support F1 scores, 0.17-0.22, also raise concerns about complete evidence retrieval and whether low RAG performance reflects reasoning difficulty or dataset/retrieval construction issues.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. Closed-source API outputs can change over time, the exact evaluated question sets and document identifiers do not appear to be clearly released, and important reranker fine-tuning details such as dataset size, hyperparameters, and training configuration are missing.

Some claims are overextended relative to the evidence. The experiments use only the English Wikipedia corpus, but the paper claims particular value for specialized domains and scarce-resource settings without testing those settings, and the cross-language claim is left entirely to future work.
The truncated radar chart, scaled from 3.0 to 4.5 rather than the stated full 1-to-5 scale, visually exaggerates differences between systems despite the caption's disclosure.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: automatically creating verifiable cross-document multi-hop QA data from raw corpora could substantially reduce annotation cost and support domains with limited resources.

The pipeline is conceptually coherent and covers both major reasoning patterns: bridge questions and comparison questions. It combines entity-driven query formulation, diversity-aware retrieval, reranking, sub-question composition, attribute filtering, and final validation.

The paper explicitly targets fact distribution and no-shortcut requirements and retains reasoning paths and supporting evidence, making outputs more inspectable than many purely prompt-based question generators.

The evaluation is broader than typical question-generation studies. It combines LLM-as-judge scoring, judge-reliability analysis, Q-only versus Q+golden-document answering, retrieval accessibility, reranker and polisher ablations, manual inspection, cost analysis, and end-to-end RAG evaluation.

Results provide encouraging evidence that the generated questions are grounded and challenging: adding golden documents produces large solver gains, manually inspected reasoning paths are correct in 92% of cases, the 500-sample validation is consistent with the main results, and current RAG systems remain far from solving the data.

Reproducibility is supported by named models, deterministic generation settings, retrieval parameters, the Wikipedia snapshot, cost estimates, extensive prompt documentation, and a stated intention to release code.
The paper is clearly written, with helpful framework diagrams, formal definitions in the appendix, concrete synthesized examples, and detailed limitations.
weaknesses: The strongest claims—especially “first” without human intervention and quality that meets or exceeds human-annotated datasets—are somewhat overstated. The main quality study uses only about 100 samples, reports no confidence intervals or significance tests, and the advantages over HotpotQA are very small for several settings. LLM judges may also systematically favor fluent LLM-generated questions.

The human validation is useful but limited: it uses three student raters, 50 pairwise comparisons selected to have non-trivial score gaps, and yields Fleiss’ κ of only 0.46. It supports ranking reliability but does not establish blind absolute superiority over human datasets.

There is no end-to-end comparison with a prior automatic question-generation pipeline. The paper compares only with human datasets and ablates internal components, so it does not isolate how much HopWeaver improves over alternative LLM-based synthesis approaches.

Authentic multi-hop necessity is primarily established through LLM judgment and a 100-question manual audit. A systematic empirical shortcut test—for example, attempting to answer each question from either document alone—is missing, despite being the most direct validation of the no-shortcut constraint.

The very low Support F1 scores (approximately 0.17–0.22) indicate that retrieving the complete evidence bundle is difficult. The paper should more clearly separate retrieval difficulty from reasoning difficulty and discuss whether this makes the resulting benchmark impractical for some evaluation settings.

Generalization is narrow: all main experiments are on English Wikipedia, and the paper does not deeply analyze question-template diversity, answer-type distribution, entity frequency, repetition, temporal inconsistency, or pretraining contamination/memorization.

Some reproducibility details remain incomplete in the submission, including a visible code/data URL, reranker training-set size and hyperparameters, fixed released dataset splits, and safeguards against closed-source API drift. The authors themselves note that closed-source outputs changed during the experimental period.

The RAG evaluation would benefit from larger samples, significance testing, clearer answer-normalization details, and more analysis of stylistic mismatches; format variations alone account for 36.7% of GPT-4o failures, suggesting that raw EM/F1 may confound answer formatting with reasoning ability.
